---
title: "Your first steps in R"
subtitle: "Understanding R code: values, objects, functions, vectors and missing observations"
---

::: {.callout-note title="Learning goals"}
By the end of this section, you should be able to **read a simple line of R code**, distinguish values, objects, names, functions and arguments, create and inspect vectors, select individual values, recognize common data types, and work cautiously with missing observations (`NA`). You should also be able to explain **what a number measures and what its denominator is**.
:::

## Before we begin: learning to read R code

In the previous chapter, we installed R and RStudio, created a script, and learned how to run commands. Now we will learn what those commands actually mean. We will use a small, **entirely fictional** example of asylum applications received by five administrative offices. There are only five numbers so that we can concentrate on the language instead of getting lost in a large dataset. We will work with real UNHCR data in the following chapters.

Programming involves giving the computer precise instructions. R cannot guess what we meant if we misspell a name or forget a comma. Fortunately, much of introductory R follows a small number of patterns that we can learn gradually.

### Values, calculations and results

A **value** is a piece of information. For example, `12` is a number, while `"Germany"` is a piece of text. R can immediately evaluate expressions involving values:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
12 + 18
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 30
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
(12 + 18) / 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 15
```


:::
:::


Here `+` adds, `/` divides, and parentheses indicate which calculation should be done first. R prints the result underneath the command. The `[1]` that you may see in the output is **not part of the answer**: it marks the position of the first displayed element.

For now, notice the distinction between **the command you write** and **the result R returns**. Later, we will often want to save results for reuse rather than just display them.

## Giving things names: objects and assignment

Imagine that we know an office received `12` applications. We could simply type `12` whenever we need this figure, but that quickly becomes inconvenient. Instead, we can store it under a name:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications_office_a <- 12
applications_office_a
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12
```


:::
:::


Read the first line as: *"applications_office_a gets the value 12."*

Let's break it down:

| Part of the code | What it means |
|---|---|
| `applications_office_a` | The **name** we choose |
| `<-` | The **assignment operator**: store the result on the right under the name on the left |
| `12` | The **value** being stored |
| `applications_office_a` on its own | Ask R to display the stored value |

An **object** is something stored in R's memory. A **name** is how we refer to it. You can think of a name as a label attached to a box, while the object is what is stored in that box. In practice, beginners often say *"the object `applications_office_a`"*, meaning the object referred to by that name.

Assigning a result usually does not print it. Type the object's name on a new line when you want to inspect it. You should also see the name appear in the **Environment** pane in RStudio. The Environment shows objects that exist in the current session; it is not the same thing as a saved script.

### Names are not the same as text values

Compare these two commands:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications_office_a
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
"applications_office_a"
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "applications_office_a"
```


:::
:::


The **unquoted** name asks R to retrieve the value we stored (12). The **quoted** text is simply the word `applications_office_a` itself. Quotation marks matter because R treats text and object names differently.

### Choosing clear names

You decide what to call your objects. R does not know that the word `applications` refers to asylum applications: that is a meaning **we** give the name. Good names help both you and your colleagues understand the analysis.

We recommend lowercase **snake_case**, with underscores between words:

```r
applications_2022
country_of_origin
total_refugees
```

Names are **case-sensitive**: `applications` and `Applications` are different names. Ordinary syntactic names start with a letter (or a dot not followed by a digit) and may contain letters, numbers, underscores and dots. For now, simply start with a letter and use underscores. Avoid spaces, names beginning with numbers, and names such as `mean` that could be confused with common function names.

For instance, R would not treat `total_applications` and `total_application` as the same object. A tiny typo can produce an **object not found** error.

::: {.callout-tip title="Two useful RStudio shortcuts"}
Press **Alt + -** (Windows/Linux) or **Option + -** (macOS) to insert `<-`. When typing a name you created, press **Tab** to see possible completions. Autocompletion helps avoid spelling mistakes.
:::

### Objects can be updated

Once an object exists, we can use it in a calculation and save a new result:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications_office_b <- 18
total_two_offices <- applications_office_a + applications_office_b
total_two_offices
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 30
```


:::
:::


R first finds the stored values of the two objects, adds them, and stores the result in `total_two_offices`. We could also assign a new value to an existing name:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications_office_a <- 13
applications_office_a
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 13
```


:::
:::


This **replaces the value currently associated with that name**. It does not rewrite previously executed calculations: `total_two_offices` still contains the earlier result until we calculate it again. This is one reason why running scripts from the beginning is important.

We will use a fresh vector in the next section, so this temporary change does not affect the later examples.

## One object, several values: vectors

An object does not have to contain just one number. It can also hold a **vector**, which is a sequence of values. Imagine that five fictional offices received the following numbers of asylum applications:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications <- c(12, 18, 9, 25, 16)
applications
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12 18  9 25 16
```


:::
:::


Here:

- `applications` is the name of the object.
- `<-` assigns the result to that name.
- `c()` is a function that **combines** the five values into a vector.
- The commas separate the values.
- Each value is one element of the vector.

A vector is especially useful because we can calculate with all its elements without writing separate commands for each office.

For example, multiplying by two applies to every value:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications * 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 24 36 18 50 32
```


:::
:::


This is known as a **vectorized operation**. Notice that this calculation displays new values but does **not** change `applications`. To save a result, we would assign it to an object.

::: {.callout-note title="One name does not mean one observation"}
`applications` is **one R object**, but it contains **five numbers**. An object can contain a single value, a vector of values, or even a whole table. We will distinguish tables and their columns later in this chapter.
:::

## What are functions and arguments?

R uses **functions** to carry out tasks. A function has a name followed by parentheses. We provide the information it needs inside those parentheses; this information is called its **arguments**.

Consider three functions that come with R:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
length(applications)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(applications)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 80
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(applications)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16
```


:::
:::


| Function | What it asks R to do | How to interpret the result |
|---|---|---|
| `length(applications)` | Count the elements of the vector | Five offices are represented |
| `sum(applications)` | Add the five values | Total applications across these five offices |
| `mean(applications)` | Calculate the arithmetic mean | Average applications per office |

For example, in `mean(applications)`:

- `mean` is the **function name**.
- `(` and `)` surround its arguments.
- `applications` is the **argument** supplied to the function; here it is the object holding our five numbers.

A function is different from an ordinary data object: `mean()` performs a calculation, while `applications` supplies the data. Technically, functions are also objects in R, but it is useful at this stage to distinguish the **operation** from the **data being operated on**.

### Functions can take more than one argument

Some arguments are **named**. For example, `round()` can specify how many decimal places to use:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(applications)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
round(mean(applications), digits = 1)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16
```


:::
:::


In `digits = 1`, the equals sign supplies a value to a **named function argument**. This is different from `<-`, which we use to assign an object, and `==`, which we will use to test equality.

We can put functions inside other functions. R evaluates `mean(applications)` first, then passes that result to `round()`.

::: {.callout-tip title="Useful help when writing a function"}
Type `?mean` in the Console to open the function's documentation. When you type a function followed by `(` in RStudio, it can also suggest argument names and show a short description. The examples in this chapter use base R, so you do not need an additional package for them.
:::

## Selecting elements: positions and conditions

Sometimes we only want part of a vector. We use **square brackets** `[]` to select its elements. R starts counting positions at **1**, not zero.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications[1]       # First value
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
applications[2:4]     # Second through fourth values
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 18  9 25
```


:::
:::


The part inside `[]` is called an **index**. It tells R which elements to keep. The expression `2:4` generates the positions 2, 3 and 4.

We can also ask R a question about each value:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications > 15
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
```


:::
:::


The result is a sequence of `TRUE` and `FALSE` values. This is a **logical vector**: each answer corresponds to the value at the same position in `applications`.

We can use that logical vector to select observations:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications[applications > 15]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 18 25 16
```


:::
:::


Read this as: *"From `applications`, keep only the values greater than 15."*

A few comparison symbols are particularly useful:

| Symbol | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `>` | Greater than | `18 > 15` |
| `<` | Less than | `9 < 15` |
| `>=` | Greater than or equal to | `16 >= 16` |
| `==` | Equal to | `12 == 12` |
| `!=` | Not equal to | `12 != 18` |

**Do not confuse** `<-` (assign a value) with `==` (compare values). We use `=` for named function arguments, as shown earlier.

## Different kinds of information

So far, most values have been numbers. But researchers also work with country names, years, labels, and yes/no information.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
countries <- c("Germany", "France", "Spain")
years <- c(2020, 2021, 2022)
large <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

class(countries)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "character"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(years)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "numeric"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
class(large)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "logical"
```


:::
:::


The function `class()` tells us how R classifies each object. Here, the types are **character** (text), **numeric** (numbers), and **logical** (TRUE/FALSE).

Notice the syntax:

- Country names are in quotation marks because they are text values.
- Numbers are not in quotation marks.
- `TRUE` and `FALSE` are logical values and are not in quotation marks.

The type of information matters. For example, calculating the mean of country names makes no sense, but counting how many countries meet a condition can be informative.

In these examples, each vector contains values of a single basic type. We will later work with **data frames**, whose columns may have different types.

## Missing is not zero

Imagine that one office did not provide an application count. An **unknown or unavailable value** can be represented in R by `NA`, rather than `0`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
applications_incomplete <- c(12, 18, NA, 25, 16)
applications_incomplete
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12 18 NA 25 16
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(applications_incomplete)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] NA
```


:::
:::


The mean is reported as `NA` because a missing value is present. R does not automatically assume what the missing number should have been.

We can ask R to ignore missing values for this calculation:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(applications_incomplete, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 17.75
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(is.na(applications_incomplete))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1
```


:::
:::


Let's read these unfamiliar parts:

- `na.rm` is the name of a function argument meaning **remove missing values** for the calculation.
- `TRUE` tells R to use that option.
- `is.na()` checks which elements are missing.
- `sum(is.na(...))` counts the missing entries because `TRUE` is treated as 1 when added and `FALSE` as 0.

**Crucially, `na.rm = TRUE` does not recover the missing information.** The mean now uses only the four offices with observed values. We need to ask whether those four are comparable with the missing office.

::: {.callout-warning title="A substantive distinction"}
`NA` represents a missing value in R; `0` represents a recorded zero. In refugee-statistics sources, suppressed values, noncoverage, unavailable information, and incomplete reporting may have different meanings. Never replace all missing values with zero simply because zero makes a calculation convenient. Missing-data patterns can also bias comparisons.
:::

## From vectors to tables: data frames and variables

Real datasets generally contain **several variables** describing each observation. In R, a common way to store a rectangular dataset is as a **data frame**.

Let's create one using the same fictional offices:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
practice <- data.frame(
  office = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  applications = c(12, 18, 9, 25, 16)
)
practice
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  office applications
1      A           12
2      B           18
3      C            9
4      D           25
5      E           16
```


:::
:::


This introduces an important distinction:

| Term | In our example |
|---|---|
| **Object name** | `practice` names the whole table stored in R |
| **Data frame** | The table containing offices and application counts |
| **Variable / column** | `office` and `applications` are the column names |
| **Observation / row** | Each row describes one office |
| **Unit of analysis** | An office |
| **Value / cell** | For example, `18` in the applications column for office B |

The `data.frame()` function constructs the table. Inside it, `office = ...` and `applications = ...` are **named arguments that create columns**. This is not the same as writing `applications <- ...` to create or replace an object in the wider R environment.

### A column and a separate object can have the same name

We already created a vector object named `applications`. Now our table `practice` also has a **column** called `applications`. These are distinct things.

To refer explicitly to the table's column, write:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
practice$applications
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12 18  9 25 16
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(practice$applications)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16
```


:::
:::


Read `practice$applications` as: *"the applications column belonging to the data frame `practice`."* The dollar sign `$` selects a named component of a table (or list). It is not a currency symbol here.

To inspect a data frame, useful commands include:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
names(practice)     # Column names
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "office"       "applications"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
nrow(practice)      # Number of rows
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ncol(practice)      # Number of columns
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
str(practice)       # Structure and types of columns
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
'data.frame':	5 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ office      : chr  "A" "B" "C" "D" ...
 $ applications: num  12 18 9 25 16
```


:::
:::


A row in this table corresponds to **one office**, not one individual applicant or one asylum decision. If we recorded applications for several years, we would need to specify whether one row represented an *office* or an *office-year*. This is the **unit of analysis**, and it matters for interpreting statistics.

::: {.callout-note title="A useful distinction for our future work"}
A **dataset** is the collection of information we study; a **data frame** is one way to represent that dataset in R. A **variable** is a measured characteristic, usually represented by a column. An **object** is what R stores under a name. The same data frame may contain many variables while remaining one named R object.
:::

## Calculating shares: always ask about the denominator

We can add a new column to our practice table. Suppose we want to know what percentage of the applications across these **five fictional offices** came from each office:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
practice$share <- 100 * practice$applications /
  sum(practice$applications)
practice
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  office applications share
1      A           12 15.00
2      B           18 22.50
3      C            9 11.25
4      D           25 31.25
5      E           16 20.00
```


:::
:::


Again, read the left-hand side as: *"create or update a column called `share` in `practice`."* On the right-hand side, each office's applications are divided by the **total** across the five offices, then multiplied by 100.

For example, office A contributes `12` applications out of a total of `80`, so its share is `15%`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(practice$share)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 100
```


:::
:::


The shares add up to 100%, apart from possible rounding effects. But be careful about the interpretation: the denominator is **only the five offices in our invented dataset**, not all asylum applications in a country.

::: {.callout-tip title="Every percentage needs a denominator"}
When interpreting a percentage, always ask: **"A percentage of what?"** Also ask *when*, *where*, and *for which population* the numerator and denominator were measured. Calculating a percentage correctly does not guarantee that it is a meaningful indicator.
:::

## Reading unfamiliar R code: a quick reference

Many errors arise from confusing symbols. You do not have to memorize everything at once; return to this table when needed.

| Code or symbol | Read it as | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `#` | Start of a comment | `# Fictional data` |
| `"..."` | A text value | `"Germany"` |
| `<-` | Assign to a name | `x <- 12` |
| `()` | Supply arguments to a function | `mean(applications)` |
| `c()` | Combine elements into a vector | `c(12, 18, 9)` |
| `[]` | Select elements | `applications[1]` |
| `$` | Select a named column/component | `practice$applications` |
| `==` | Check whether values are equal | `12 == 12` |
| `NA` | Missing value | `c(12, NA, 9)` |

### A common beginner error: names and capitalization

Try to predict what would happen here, but **do not execute the second line as part of rendering this book**:

```r
my_applications <- 12
My_applications
```

R will say that `My_applications` was not found. The capital `M` makes it a different name. The correction is to type `my_applications` exactly as it was created.

When in doubt, inspect the **Environment** pane and check the spelling, capitals, punctuation, and whether the line creating the object has actually run.

## Exercises: predict → run → explain

Use the script you created in the previous chapter. For each task, first **predict** what will happen, then run the code, and finally explain the result in ordinary language. All the numbers below are fictional.

### Part A. Objects and names

1. Without running it, predict the result of `mean(c(2, 4, 8))`. Then verify your answer in R.
2. Create an object named `recognitions` containing `8, 11, 3, 15, 9`. Display the vector by typing its name.
3. Explain the difference between `recognitions` and `"recognitions"`.
4. What happens if you type `Recognitions` with a capital `R`? Why?

### Part B. Functions and vectors

5. Use functions to calculate the **sum, minimum, maximum and median** of `recognitions`. Use `?median` if necessary.
6. Explain what `applications[1]` returns, compared with `applications[applications > 15]`.
7. What is the difference between `recognitions <- 10` and `recognitions == 10`? **Do not overwrite** your original vector unless you intend to; you can recreate it afterward.

### Part C. Missing values

8. Replace the **third element** of `recognitions` with `NA` using `recognitions[3] <- NA`. What happens to `mean(recognitions)`?
9. Calculate the mean again using `na.rm = TRUE`. Explain **which observations are included** and why this does not restore the missing value.

### Part D. Tables and interpretation

10. In the `practice` table, identify the **object name**, **two original variables**, **number of observations**, and **unit of analysis**.
11. Explain the difference between `applications` and `practice$applications`.
12. Create a fictional column `practice$recognized` containing `8, 11, 3, 15, 9`. Calculate `100 * practice$recognized / practice$applications` and explain what each row's percentage would represent **if** numerators and denominators referred to the same set of cases.
13. Suppose the recognition decisions occurred in the same calendar year as the application counts, but do not necessarily concern the same applicants. Is the resulting percentage necessarily a valid recognition rate? **No.** We will return to the mismatch between application cohorts and decision cohorts in the later chapter on asylum decisions.

::: {.callout-tip title="Take-home check"}
You understand this section when you can explain **what each part of a simple command does**; create and name a vector; use a function; distinguish a table from its columns; calculate a mean; and explain why a missing observation is different from a recorded zero—without copying code you do not understand.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Further reading"}
For another introduction to R expressions, assignment, comments, object names and functions, see [*R for Data Science*, Chapter 2: Workflow: basics](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/workflow-basics.html). The examples in that chapter use general data-science contexts; here we use fictional asylum-statistics examples before moving to UNHCR data.
:::
